source_text: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἅπαξ εἰς τὸν περὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἤλθομεν λόγον, Ἰουδαίοις μὲν, τοῖς πιστεύουσι θείῳ πνεύματι αὐτοὺς λελαληκέναι, οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἔσται ἀχρήσιμα τὰ ἐποισθησόμενα (ἀλλὰ) καὶ τοῖς εὐγνωμονοῦσι δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων. πρὸς οὓς ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ἀναγκαῖον παραδέξασθαι ὅτι καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι προφήτας εἶχον, εἴπερ ἔμελλον συνέχεσθαι ἐν τῇ δοθείσῃ αὐτοῖς νομοθεσίᾳ καὶ πιστεύειν τῷ δημιουργῷ, καθάπερ εἰλήφεισαν, καὶ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ νόμῳ μὴ ἔχειν ἀφορμὰς ἀποστῆναι εἰς τὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν πολυθεότητα. τὸ δ᾿ ἀναγκαῖον οὕτω παραστήσομεν. „τὰ ἔθνη,“ ὡς γέγραπται καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ τῶν Ἰουδαίων νόμῳ, „κληδόνων καὶ μαντειῶν ἀκούσονται“· τῷ δὲ λαῷ ἐκείνῳ εἴρηται· „σοὶ δὲ οὐχ οὕτως ἔδωκε κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ καὶ ἐπιφέρεται τούτῳ τὸ „προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ εἴπερ οὖν τῶν ἐθνῶν χρωμένων μαντείαις εἴτε διὰ „κληδόνων“ εἴτε δι᾿ οἰωνῶν εἴτε δι᾿ ὀρνίθων εἴτε δι᾿ ἐγγαστριμύθων εἴτε καὶ διὰ τῶν τὴν θυτικὴν ἐπαγγελλομένων εἴτε καὶ διὰ Χαλδαίων γενεθλιαλογούντων, ἅπερ πάντα Ἰουδαίοις ἀπείρητο. Ἰουδαῖοι εἰ μηδεμίαν εἶχον παραμυθίαν γνώσεως τῶν μελλόντων, ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἂν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης περὶ τὴν γνῶσιν λιχνείας τῶν ἐσομένων ἀγόμενοι κατεφρόνησαν μὲν ἂν τῶν ἰδίων ὡς οὐδὲν ἐχόντων θεῖον ἐν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ οὐκ ἂν μετὰ Μω(??)σέα προφήτην προσήκαντο οὐδ᾿ ἀνέγραψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς λόγους, αὐτόμολοι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν μαντεῖα καὶ χρηστήρια μετέστησαν ἢ ἐπεχείρησαν ἂν ἱδρῦσαί τι τοιοῦτον καὶ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς. ὥστ᾿ οὐδὲν ἄτοπόν ἐστι καὶ περὶ τῶν τυχόντων τοὺς παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς προφήτας εἰς παραμυθίαν τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ποθούντων προειρηκέναι, ὥστε καὶ „περὶ ὄνων ἀπολωλυιῶν“ προφητεύειν τὸν Σαμουὴλ καὶ περὶ νόσου παιδὸς βασιλικοῦ τὸν ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν Βασιλειῶν ἀναγεγραμμένον. πῶς δ᾿ ἂν τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων μαντείαν λαβεῖν ἐπέπλησσον οἱ τὰ τοῦ νόμου Ἰουδαίων πρεσβεύοντες; ὥσπερ εὑρίσκεται Ἠλίας τῷ Ὀχοζίᾳ ἐπιπλήσσων καὶ λέγων· „εἰ παρὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι θεὸν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ὑμεῖς πορεύεσθε ἐκζητῆσαι ἐν τῇ Βαὰλ μυῖαν θεὸν Ἀκκαρῶν.“
pass_a_gloss: Since we have once come to the discourse about the prophets, for the Jews, who believe that they spoke by the divine Spirit, the things that will be said will not be useless, but also for the Greeks who are well-disposed. To whom we will say that it is necessary to accept that the Jews also had prophets, if indeed they were going to be held together in the law given to them and believe in the Creator, just as they had received, and not have a starting point to revolt to the polytheism of the nations. We will present the necessary thing in this way. 'The nations', as it is written also in the law of the Jews, 'will hear of divinations and omens'; but to that people it is said: 'The Lord your God has not given you such things.' And it is added to this: 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers.' If, then, the nations use divinations, either through 'divinations' or through birds or through entrails or through ventriloquists or through those who promise sacrifices or through Chaldeans who calculate births, all of which were forbidden to the Jews, the Jews would not have had any consolation of knowledge of future things, they would have been led by the same human curiosity about knowledge of future things, they would have despised their own as having nothing divine in themselves, and they would not have followed Moses as a prophet, nor would they have written down their words, but they would have deserted to the divinations and oracles of the nations or would have tried to establish something like this among themselves. So it is not absurd that the prophets among them spoke for the consolation of those who long for such things, so that even Samuel prophesied about donkeys that had been lost and the one written in the third book of Kings prophesied about the illness of a royal child. How would the Jewish elders, who preside over the law, have rebuked someone who wanted to take divination from idols? Just as Elijah is found rebuking Ohozias, saying: 'If it is not because there is no God in Israel, you go to consult the fly god of Ekron.'

bible_refs.note: The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers

pass_b_english: Since we have turned to the subject of the prophets, what follows will not be useless for the Jews, who believe the prophets spoke by the divine Spirit — and it will also serve the well-disposed among the Greeks. We will tell them that they must accept that the Jews had prophets too, if the Jews were indeed to remain bound together in the law given them, to believe in the Creator just as they had received him, and to have no opening to revolt into the polytheism of the nations. We will establish this necessity as follows. 'The nations,' as it is written even in the law of the Jews themselves, 'will listen to diviners and soothsayers'; but to that people it was said: 'The Lord your God has not given you such things' (Deuteronomy 18:14). And this is added to it: 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers' (Deuteronomy 18:15). Now if the nations resort to divination — whether by omens, or by watching birds, or by reading entrails, or through ventriloquists, or through those who promise sacrificial rites, or through Chaldean astrologers — all of which were forbidden to the Jews — then, if the Jews had possessed no consolation of foreknowledge, they would have been driven by the same human craving to know the future. They would have despised their own heritage as having nothing divine in it; they would not have followed Moses as a prophet, nor recorded their words, but would have deserted to the divinations and oracles of the nations, or even tried to set up something similar among themselves. Therefore it is not absurd that the prophets among them spoke beforehand for the consolation of those who long for such knowledge — so that even Samuel prophesied about lost donkeys, and the prophet recorded in the third book of Kings spoke about the illness of a royal child (2 Kings 1:2–3). How else would the Jewish elders, who represent the law, have rebuked anyone who wanted to seek divination from idols? Just as Elijah is found rebuking Ahaziah and saying: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?' (2 Kings 1:3).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the required scripture citations for the quoted/alluded passages (Deuteronomy 18:14, 18:15; 2 Kings 1:2-3, 1:3), which is a required addition for the reviewer. Pass A is a faithful translation of the Greek. The translation of 'γενεθλιαλογούντων' as 'calculate births' (Pass A) and 'astrologers' (Pass B) is acceptable within the context of Chaldean practices. The uncertainty in the Greek 'Μω(??)σέα' is handled by the translators.
